evidence.claim: Construction began in 1946 to connect the Kenai Peninsula’s agricultural area with Seward, improving transport for farms and opening the area to tourism.
evidence.quote: To assist in agricultural transport and also open areas to tourism, work began on the Sterling Highway in 1946 to connect the Kenai Peninsula agricultural area with Seward.

evidence.claim: The road first carried traffic in winter 1950, when freezing temperatures made the unfinished surface passable.
evidence.quote: The Sterling Highway opened to traffic during the winter of 1950, when temperatures below freezing made it possible to travel over the unfinished surface.

evidence.claim: Grading and gravel were needed before summer traffic could use it the following year. Full paving followed in 1958.
evidence.quote: However, the highway required grading and gravel surfacing before being ready for summer traffic the following year. The highway was fully paved in 1958.

evidence.claim: The highway honors Hawley W. Sterling, an engineer whose service as assistant chief engineer lasted from 1932 until his death in 1948.
evidence.quote: This highway honors Hawley W. Sterling, lifetime ARC engineer who served as assistant chief engineer from 1932 until his death in 1948.

evidence.claim: Start at Tern Lake Junction on the Seward Highway and follow Kenai Lake to Cooper Landing.
evidence.quote: leading from the Seward Highway at Tern Lake Junction

evidence.claim: Start at Tern Lake Junction on the Seward Highway and follow Kenai Lake to Cooper Landing.
evidence.quote: Drive along the ice blue-green Kenai Lake until you get to Cooper Landing.

evidence.claim: The highway continues west beside the Kenai River to Soldotna, then turns south along Cook Inlet.
evidence.quote: It leads mainly west from Tern Lake to Soldotna, paralleling the Kenai River, at which point it turns south to follow the eastern shore of Cook Inlet.

evidence.claim: From Anchor Point, Route 1 leads southeast to Homer.
evidence.quote: Alaska Route 1 runs southeast from Anchor Bay 15 miles (24 km) to Homer

evidence.claim: The road ends at the tip of Homer Spit, 4.5 miles into Kachemak Bay, where a ferry terminal connects with the Alaska Marine Highway.
evidence.quote: The southern end of the highway is at the tip of the Homer Spit, a landspit extending 4.5 miles (7.2 km) into Kachemak Bay. A ferry terminal here connects the road to the Alaska Marine Highway.

evidence.claim: Cooper Landing occupies the outlet where Kenai Lake becomes the Kenai River.
evidence.quote: at the outlet of Kenai Lake into the Kenai River.

evidence.claim: Its name recalls Joseph Cooper’s 1884 gold discovery, though Russian engineer Peter Doroshin had identified gold prospects in 1848.
evidence.quote: Cooper Landing was named for Joseph Cooper, a miner who discovered gold there in 1884. However, Peter Doroshin, a Russian engineer, had identified gold prospects as far back as 1848

evidence.claim: Road connections expanded in stages: east to Seward in 1938, west to Kenai in 1948 and north to Anchorage by 1951.
evidence.quote: In 1938, a road was constructed east to Seward. In 1948, a road west to Kenai was opened, and by 1951, residents could drive north to Anchorage.

evidence.claim: The former post office began as a simple log cabin and grew through additions in the 1920s and 1930s.
evidence.quote: as a simple log cabin, and was enlarged in the 1920s and 1930s

evidence.claim: Caribou and moose antlers decorate its facade.
evidence.quote: Its facade is adorned with hunting trophies such as caribou and moose antlers.

evidence.claim: The building and the historic school were moved a short distance west and became part of the Cooper Landing Historical Museum.
evidence.quote: The building has been relocated a short distance to the west, along with the historical Ridderford School, and is now part of the Cooper Landing Historical Museum.

evidence.claim: Anchor Point reaches the westernmost point of the contiguous highway system.
evidence.quote: Anchor Point is the western most point of the contiguous highway system

evidence.claim: Its English name comes from a legend that Captain James Cook lost an anchor here.
evidence.quote: The name "Anchor Point" comes from a legend that when Captain James Cook discovered the area, he lost an anchor.

evidence.claim: The Anchor River runs through the community and enters Cook Inlet just west of its center.
evidence.quote: The Anchor River runs through the southern part of the CDP, entering Cook Inlet just west of the town center.

evidence.claim: The river supports wild salmon and steelhead runs, which Alaska’s transportation department highlights in its description of the southern byway.
evidence.quote: home of Anchor River and its wild salmon and steelhead runs.

evidence.claim: There is no harbor; a beach service uses tractors to launch boats into deeper water and retrieve them.
evidence.quote: Anchor Point does not have a harbor, but it has a boat-launch service at the beach that uses tractors to launch and recover boats from shore to deeper water.

evidence.claim: From the recreation-area beach, the view includes the distant volcanic peaks of Mount Augustine, Mount Iliamna and Mount Redoubt.
evidence.quote: From the beach at the recreation area you can see the distant peaks of the Aleutian Range, including the volcanoes Mount Augustine, Mount Iliamna, and Mount Redoubt.

evidence.claim: Homer Spit carries the highway’s final miles into Kachemak Bay.
evidence.quote: The southern end of the highway is at the tip of the Homer Spit, a landspit extending 4.5 miles (7.2 km) into Kachemak Bay.

evidence.claim: In 1899, the Cook Inlet Coal Fields Company laid railroad track along it to connect the docks with coal fields beside the bay.
evidence.quote: In 1899, the Cook Inlet Coal Fields Company laid a railroad track along the spit, connecting the docks to the coal fields along Kachemak Bay.

evidence.claim: That business helped generate the settlement that became Homer.
evidence.quote: The resulting business led to the development of what eventually became Homer, Alaska.

evidence.claim: The 1964 earthquake reduced the spit’s area and killed most of its vegetation, leaving a surface dominated by gravel and sand.
evidence.quote: The 1964 Alaska earthquake shrank it to 508 acres (2.06 km2), and killed most of the vegetation, making it today mostly gravel and sand.

evidence.claim: The spit now holds Homer Boat Harbor, with deep- and shallow-water docks serving commercial and pleasure boats.
evidence.quote: The spit is also home to the Homer Boat Harbor. The harbor contains both deep and shallow water docks and serves up to 1500 commercial and pleasure boats at its summer peak.

evidence.claim: At the highway’s end, the ferry terminal connects road travel with the Alaska Marine Highway.
evidence.quote: A ferry terminal here connects the road to the Alaska Marine Highway.
